planting.note: Move outdoors to a sheltered, humid shade spot only after nights stay reliably above 60F; otherwise keep as a year-round indoor terrarium or greenhouse subject.

directions: A dwarf Bornean species valued by collectors for its compact rosette of thick, deeply quilted, dark olive-green leaves with a satiny, almost pebbled surface. Grow in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix and keep humidity high, since the small stature makes it prone to drying out faster than larger-leaved relatives. Give it bright, filtered shade rather than deep shadow to keep leaf texture pronounced, and avoid letting the compact rhizome sit in standing water. It is slow to bulk up, so division is the most reliable propagation method once offsets form.
sources: International Aroid Society — The Genus Alocasia

planting.note: Best kept as a permanent warm-greenhouse or indoor collector plant outside true tropical climates.

directions: Native to Sarawak and closely allied to Alocasia scabriuscula and A. princeps, this species forms an upright shrub-like clump with arrow-shaped, dark-stemmed leaves marked by pale, contrasting primary veins. Plant in a well-aerated bark-and-perlite aroid mix and provide steady warmth, high humidity, and bright shade to keep the dark petioles and leaf blades from scorching. Water as the top layer of mix begins to dry, and avoid cold drafts, which cause rapid leaf drop. It is a slow-spreading rhizomatous species best propagated by division of established offsets.
sources: International Aroid Society — The Genus Alocasia

planting.note: Needs a large container or shaded bed with room to spread; not practical for small indoor collections.

directions: One of the largest-leaved Alocasia species known, endemic to Borneo, producing enormous arrow-shaped blades on thick, towering petioles once mature. Site it in deep, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in filtered shade with high ambient humidity, mimicking the understory of lowland rainforest. Give it generous space and shelter from wind, since the oversized leaves tear easily, and feed regularly through the warm season to support its rapid, massive growth. It is essentially a specialist botanical-garden or large-greenhouse subject in temperate climates, overwintered under cover where it is not hardy.
sources: International Aroid Society — The Genus Alocasia

planting.note: Train on a moss pole or allow to trail; grown outdoors only in frost-free zones.

directions: Native from Mexico through Central America, this climbing aroid earns its common name 'fivefingers' from the deeply divided, hand-like leaf lobes it develops once mature, a dramatic contrast to its simple arrowhead-shaped juvenile leaves. Grow it in bright indirect to moderate light with a well-drained, humus-rich mix, and let it climb a support or trail from a hanging basket to encourage the more deeply lobed adult foliage. Keep soil lightly moist but never soggy, and provide a humid microclimate to prevent brown leaf-tip dieback. Propagate easily from stem cuttings rooted in water or moist medium.
sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service — Species Profile
University of South Florida — Atlas of Florida Plants

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or warm-greenhouse climber; often confused with the similar S. macrophyllum in the trade.

directions: A climbing understory species from southern Mexico and Guatemala, grown for its glossy, substantial, broadly arrow-shaped leaves and compact habit compared to the more common Syngonium podophyllum. Pot it in a loose, well-aerated aroid mix and let it climb a totem or spill from an elevated container, keeping it out of direct sun to avoid bleached, pale foliage. Water when the surface of the mix dries slightly, and maintain warmth and humidity above typical household levels for the best leaf sheen. Cuttings with at least one node root readily in water within a few weeks.
sources: Revista de la Sociedad Mexicana de Historia Natural

planting.note: Keep as an indoor or warm-greenhouse foliage plant; grows in a more restrained, upright habit than the common cultivated Dieffenbachia types.

directions: A South American subshrub species, native across northwestern Brazil, Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela, notable among Dieffenbachia for its proportionally narrower, smaller leaf blades and slimmer cane-like stems. Grow it in a loose, well-drained potting mix in bright, filtered shade, watering when the top of the soil dries and reducing frequency in cooler months. Like other Dieffenbachia, its sap is irritating and the plant is toxic if chewed or ingested, so site it away from curious pets and children. Stem cuttings with a node root readily in moist medium to produce new plants.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden — Annals (Revision of Dieffenbachia)
International Aroid Society — The Genus Dieffenbachia

planting.note: Compact habit suits terrariums and small pots; overwinter indoors well above 55F.

directions: Native to southern Myanmar and southern Thailand, this miniature Aglaonema species forms a tight, low clump of slender, marbled, silvery-gray-green leaves distinctly smaller than the hybrid Aglaonema cultivars common in the trade. Grow it in bright, indirect light in a well-drained mix, allowing the surface to dry slightly between waterings to avoid stem rot in its compact crown. It tolerates low indoor light but keeps its best marbling with a bit more brightness, and benefits from steady warmth and moderate humidity year-round. Divide basal offsets once a clump has filled its pot.

planting.note: Prefers consistently wet, boggy soil; suited to pond margins or saucer culture in frost-free gardens.

directions: Ranging from southeastern Mexico south to Colombia, this peace lily species naturally grows along stream banks and in seasonally flooded swamp forest, giving it a higher tolerance for waterlogged soil than the common florist Spathiphyllum wallisii. Its narrow, lance-shaped leaves and slender white spathes give it a more graceful, grassy look than bushier hybrid peace lilies. Keep the growing medium constantly moist to wet, never letting it dry out, and provide warm temperatures and deep shade to moderate filtered light. Divide crowded clumps at the crown to propagate new plants.

planting.note: A larger-growing peace lily species for humid shade gardens or large containers in frost-free zones.

directions: Widespread across northern South America, including Brazil, Colombia, the Guianas, Peru, and Venezuela, this species produces broader, more substantial leaf blades and a larger overall habit than the compact florist peace lily cultivars. Grow it in rich, consistently moist soil in deep to filtered shade, mimicking its native wet tropical forest floor habitat, and keep humidity high to prevent leaf-edge browning. It tolerates brief periods of standing water better than most houseplant aroids, making it suitable for bog gardens in warm climates. Established clumps are easily increased by division at the base.

planting.note: Give it a moss pole or similar support to climb; grown as a houseplant or warm-greenhouse climber outside the tropics.

directions: Found from Brazil and Colombia to Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela, this climbing species takes its name from the distinctive panduriform, or fiddle-shaped, outline its mature leaves develop, with a pinched waist partway along each blade quite unlike its juvenile heart-shaped leaves. Grow it climbing a totem in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix, in bright indirect to moderate light, and let the top layer of mix dry before watering again. High humidity and warm, draft-free conditions help it push the more dramatically lobed adult foliage rather than staying in juvenile form indefinitely. Stem cuttings with aerial roots or a node establish readily in a humid propagation setup.
